procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the Appellate Bench of the High Court of Madras dated September 12, 1967, which reversed the orders of a single Judge (Kailasam, J.) and granted the reliefs prayed for by the respondents.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court of Madras under Art. 226 of the Constitution, seeking to quash show-cause notices issued by the Deputy Collector of Customs, Visakhapatnam, and to prohibit further action based on those notices. A single Judge (Kailasam, J.) dismissed the petitions on September 1, 1966. On appeal, a Divisional Bench (Appellate Bench) allowed the petitions on September 12, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Union of India, the Collector of Customs, Madras, and the Deputy Collector of Customs, Visakhapatnam (referred to as 'appellants' in the text) appealed to the Supreme Court after obtaining the necessary certificates from the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether on the facts set out in the show cause notices, the respondents can be held to have contravened s. 12(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947.

facts: The respondents were exporters of manganese ore.
They were accused of under-invoicing their exports and failing to repatriate foreign exchange worth about three crores of rupees.
Before exporting, the respondents submitted declarations in the prescribed form to the Collector of Customs, as required by law.
The Collector of Customs accepted these declarations and passed the goods for shipment.
Subsequently, the authorities issued a show-cause notice alleging that the declarations were deliberately false and fraudulent, and therefore the export was in violation of the law.
law: Section 12(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, along with a government notification, prohibited the export of goods unless the exporter furnished a declaration to the prescribed authority.
This declaration had to state that the amount representing the 'full export value' of the goods would be paid and repatriated.
The government's position was that a fraudulent declaration is no declaration at all, and thus the export was made in violation of the prohibition under s. 12(1).
application: The Supreme Court focused on the specific wording of Section 12(1), which required that a declaration be 'furnished' before export.
The Court found that the respondents had, in fact, furnished the required declarations to the customs authorities before each shipment.
The Court drew a distinction between the act of furnishing a declaration (which complies with s. 12(1)) and the act of furnishing a *false* declaration.

It reasoned that while furnishing a false declaration might be an offense under other provisions of the Act (such as Section 22, which specifically penalizes giving false information), it did not constitute a contravention of Section 12(1) itself.

The Division Bench of the High Court, whose decision was effectively upheld, had reasoned that since the declarations were made and scrutinized by the authorities, it could not be said that the goods were exported in violation of the prohibition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that on the facts alleged in the show-cause notice, the respondents could not be considered to have contravened Section 12(1) of the Act. Because they had furnished the required declarations before exporting, they had complied with the procedural requirement of that specific section, even if the contents of those declarations were allegedly false.

arguments.issue_text: Whether on the facts set out in the show cause notices, the respondents can be held to have contravened s. 12(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947.
appellant_arguments: The respondents engaged in a fraudulent scheme to deliberately undervalue exported goods in their declarations, inducing the department to accept them through false evidence and suppression of facts.
This scheme resulted in a failure to repatriate a significant amount of foreign exchange that had been earned surreptitiously.

This act of filing a deliberately false declaration constitutes a contravention of s. 12(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, and by virtue of s. 23A, it is an offence under s. 167(8) of the Sea Customs Act.
respondent_arguments: The filing of a declaration with the Collector of Customs was sufficient compliance with the statutory provisions of s. 12(1).
The Collector of Customs had scrutinized and passed the consignments for shipment based on these declarations.
Once the consignments were passed, the Collector had no further jurisdiction to take proceedings against them for that export.

cases.principle: Where a statute enables an authority to make regulations, a regulation made under the Act becomes for the purpose of obedience or disobedience a provision of the Act.

cases.case_name: Re H. P. C. Productions Ltd.
cases.principle: For the true rule of construction of a penal section, which involves looking at surrounding circumstances, the mischief to be remedied, the words used, and applying principles for penal statutes if there is ambiguity.

The proper approach to statutory construction is to look at all the surrounding circumstances, the mischief intended to be remedied, and to give effect to the words that have been used in the section.
If, after construing a penal statute, there appears any reasonable doubt or ambiguity, the court must apply the principles of strict construction for penal statutes.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When interpreting a penal section of a statute, it is not competent for a court to stretch the language of the provision in order to carry out the intention of the Legislature.
obiter: Where a statute enables an authority to make regulations, a regulation made under the Act becomes a provision of the Act for the purpose of obedience or disobedience.
Regulations made under an Act must be read as though they were contained in the Act itself.
The proper approach to the construction of a statute is to look at all the surrounding circumstances, the mischief intended to be remedied, and to give effect to the words that have been used.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the facts set out in the show cause notice, the respondents could not be held to have contravened s. 12(1). The court found that the language of s. 12(1) does not permit the interpretation placed on it by the appellants, and it was not convinced that the legislature intended for the offenses complained of to be made punishable under s. 23(A).
legal_tests_applied: s. 12(1) is a penal section, and in interpreting it it is not competent to the Court to stretch its language in order to carry out the intention of the Legislature.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that the language of s. 12(1) does not permit the acceptance of the interpretation placed on it by the appellants.
The court was unable to conclude that the legislature intended that the offences complained of in these proceedings should be made punishable under s. 23(A).
why_respondent_won: The court interpreted s. 12(1) as a penal section and refused to stretch its language to include the conduct alleged by the appellants, even if it was done to carry out the broader intention of the Legislature.
policy_considerations: While the regulations in the Act are enacted in the economic and financial interest of the country and their rigour should be maintained, this does not permit a court to stretch the language of a penal section.
If the interpretation sought to be placed by the appellants on s. 12(1) is accepted it may result in unnecessary hardship in numerous cases.
